$comment: The engine-neutrality ratchet. One entry per directory under src/, recording how much of it
still names a JavaScript engine directly. scripts/check-engine-neutrality.sh measures the tree
and compares it against these numbers.
THESE NUMBERS MAY FALL AND MAY NEVER RISE. A count above its budget fails the build, and the
fix is to port the file rather than to raise the number. A migration that moves a file onto
Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal lowers a count, and must lower the budget in the SAME COMMIT -- the
check reports every count that came in under budget for exactly that reason, because a ratchet
nobody tightens is a ratchet that stops at whatever the worst day was.
THE ONE RISE THAT IS NOT A REGRESSION IS A CHANGE TO THE METRIC, AND THERE HAS BEEN ONE.
engineReferences used to count only the string 'Broiler.JavaScript'. Every project under src/
has a RootNamespace beginning 'Broiler.', so 'JavaScript.Runtime.JSObject' compiles and means
the same thing -- and 23 real references in Broiler.HtmlBridge.Dom were spelled that way,
invisible to the check, concentrated in exactly the files mid-migration where somebody had
dropped a using and qualified what was left. The count now sees both spellings. Dom's recorded
number therefore went 108 -> 111 in the commit that widened it while its actual coupling FELL by
18 in the same commit, and both halves of that sentence are the point: a number may rise when
the instrument improves, and it may never rise because the tree got worse. A commit doing the
first says so here.
The consequence worth stating plainly: a project whose budget is already 0 cannot gain an
engine-coupled file at all. That is the state every entry here is travelling towards, and it
is what lets the remaining migration land as a hundred small changes instead of one merge that
moves 250 files and can only be reviewed by trusting it.
Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal is 0/0/0 and is the one entry these numbers do not actually protect.
Its project file has no ProjectReference and no PackageReference, so an assembly that cannot
see a Broiler.JavaScript type cannot name one: its neutrality is a compiler outcome, not a grep
result. What the check guards there is the CLAIM -- it fails if that project file ever gains a
reference of either kind, because the moment it does, every 0 below stops meaning anything.
WHAT EACH METRIC COUNTS, LITERALLY.
engineReferences   Occurrences of the text 'Broiler.JavaScript' in .cs files beneath the
directory, bin/ and obj/ excluded. Text, not semantics: a using directive,
a fully-qualified type name and a mention inside a doc comment each count
one. Counting occurrences rather than files is deliberate -- a file being
half-ported is progress, and a metric that only moved when a whole file
landed would hide it.
engineProjectRefs  ProjectReference Include paths in the directory's .csproj files that point
into Broiler.JS/ or Broiler.VM/, counted regardless of Condition. This is
the metric that actually has to reach 0 for an engine to be swappable: as
long as a binding project links the engine, nothing stops the next file
from using it, and the two counts above are the only thing noticing.
guestEvalSites     Occurrences of '.Eval(' in .cs files. The name records where these are
going, not what they are: today's sites are undifferentiated, and splitting
them into IJsSource.EvaluateHostScript (source this repository authored,
exempt from the page's content policy) and EvaluateGuestSource (source the
page supplied, which a Content-Security-Policy may forbid) is the porting
work this number measures. A ported site names neither .Eval( nor an engine
type, so it leaves all three counts at once.
WHY THE UNIT IS A DIRECTORY AND NOT A PROJECT FILE. src/Broiler.App has no .csproj: its eight
files are pulled in by <Compile Include="..\Broiler.App\..."> from three heads. Keying this
on project files would leave those files counted nowhere, which is the one place an engine
reference could be parked without any budget noticing. Keying on the directory covers them, and
makes the entry name the same string the check prints.
This is an object rather than the array eng/solutions.json uses, so that a directory cannot be
budgeted twice -- two entries for one project would let the check read whichever came first.

A project marked "role": "provider" is the one kind whose engine references are SUPPOSED to grow -- naming the engine is what a provider assembly is for. For those, engineReferences and guestEvalSites are recorded and reported when they drift, but not enforced; engineProjectRefs stays enforced, because which engine assemblies a provider links is a real boundary and a Broiler.JS provider quietly acquiring a Broiler.VM reference should have to argue for it in a diff.

Broiler.App.note: Shared sources with no project file of their own; linked into the Core, Linux and Windows heads. Nothing here has ever touched the engine, and being at 0 without a csproj means it cannot acquire a reference except in source.

Broiler.Browser.Core.note: The one reference is Broiler.JavaScript.All, unconditional. No source here names the engine, so this is a link the head does not use directly -- it is here because BrowserApp.NewScriptEngine() still picks an engine with an #if rather than through JsEngineRegistry. It drops to 0 when it does; see the remarks on JsEngineRegistry. The sibling reference to Broiler.HtmlBridge.Scripting.Vm is conditional on the -VM build types and is not counted, because it points inside src/.

Broiler.Browser.Core.Tests.note: ONE, AND THE ARGUMENT THIS ENTRY ASKED FOR IS BELOW. It used to read: 'if a test ever needs to name one directly, that is a real budget increase and this file is where the argument for it belongs.' JsInteropSeamTests is that test. JsInterop is the seam between an engine object and a JSEAL handle, and its defect was that a function crossing it came back kind Object while the same function from the provider came back kind Function -- so two handles over one object compared unequal, which a handle-keyed map cannot survive. A test that could not name JSObject could not assert the correspondence; it could only assert that JSEAL agrees with itself. The increase is one using line and it buys the only check that would catch the defect returning. It falls back to 0 when JsInterop is deleted, which is the whole point of the programme this test serves. VmScriptEngineTests still compiles only under the -VM build types and gets the engine transitively.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Core.note: ONE FILE, ONE LINE, AND IT IS THE SEAM. The single reference is `using Broiler.JavaScript.Engine;` in Dom/IDomBridgeRuntime.cs, and the only thing it serves is the pair of Attach overloads that take a JSContext. This was 3 across two files until ScriptCompileAhead.cs was deleted -- 327 lines with no caller anywhere in the tree, whose two usings were the other 2. What that removal buys is not the count: it means engineProjectRefs 1, the ProjectReference to Broiler.JavaScript.Engine, is now held by exactly one API in one file, so an Attach that takes an IJsRealm drops the reference in the same commit rather than turning up a second dependency behind it. This is the highest-value entry in the file despite being the smallest -- an Attach a second engine can call is what makes a second engine able to serve a page at all. Note for whoever ports it: Broiler.JS's own docs/roadmap/Modernization.md MOD-M5 names the deleted file as an import source, so it is taken from this repository's history rather than from the tree.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Dom.note: 44 -> 43 BY DELETING ANOTHER MEMBER HELD OPEN BY A DOC COMMENT NAMING A CALLER IT DID NOT HAVE. DomBridge.WindowContext.cs carried two RunWithWindowContext overloads, one taking the engine's object and one taking a handle, and the remarks above them said the engine-typed one was kept for the sub-document script runner in DomBridge/SubDocuments.cs. That call site is one unchanged line and it has bound to the handle overload ever since SubWindowBinding.GetOrCreate was re-typed to answer one -- FrameScriptExecutionTests was written to cover precisely that rebinding and says so in its header, so the tree carried its own disproof in a second file. The only caller the engine-typed overload actually had was DomBridge.MessagingHost.cs, which unwrapped a handle to an engine object so the overload could wrap the same object straight back before handing it to WindowContextManager, whose single RunWithWindowContext has taken a handle all along. The round trip was unobservable and that is checkable rather than assumed: both callers of IMessagingHost.RunWithWindowContext are guarded to objects (MessagingBinding.RunInOwnerWindow returns early unless IsObject, and WindowPostMessage falls back to the installed window handle when call.This is not one), and JsInterop.FromEngineObject now answers the kind the provider would, so the trip was identity in reference and in kind for every value that could reach it. One occurrence moves, in one file: the using line the deleted parameter needed. DomBridge.WindowContext.cs 1 -> 0, and JsInterop. crossings 93 -> 91. 49 -> 48, AND THE ONE OCCURRENCE THAT WENT WAS A using LINE THAT EIGHTEEN CALL SITES IN FIFTEEN OTHER FILES WERE KEEPING ALIVE. FindDomNodeByJSObject and FindDomElementByJSObject in DomBridge/Utilities.cs took the engine's object; every caller held a JSEAL handle, unwrapped it at its own seam, and the pair wrapped it straight back up to ask a registry that has been keyed on JsValue.ObjectIdentity since it was re-typed. Both now take the handle. That deleted 19 JsInterop crossings (97 -> 78 by grep -o) and left fifteen files with none at all, but the ratchet could only ever see the one using -- which is the same lesson Runtime/JsInterop.cs records and the reason 49 falls by 1 and not by 19. The names still spell the type they no longer take; renaming them moves no count and is a separate change. TWO THROWS STOP HAPPENING, NOT ONE, AND THEY ARE UNREACHABLE FOR DIFFERENT REASONS. JsInterop.ToEngineObject is `ReferenceOf(value) as JSObject ?? throw`, and its own doc comment names both causes: a primitive, or a handle from a realm of another engine. (a) THE PRIMITIVE. Eight of the eighteen sites have no IsObject guard of their own, and all eight are called only from module frames that do guard, verified caller by caller, so no page reaches the old throw or the new null. (b) THE FOREIGN REALM. Under a non-Broiler.JS realm every one of the eighteen throws today whatever the guards say, because `as JSObject` is null for a handle another engine minted; after this commit they resolve through JsObjectRegistry by ObjectIdentity, which is engine-neutral. THAT IS PROGRESS TOWARD A SECOND ENGINE AND NOT A SECOND ENGINE: the bridge still refuses one earlier, at DomBridge/Registration/Registration.cs:131, which is the same ToEngineObject call inside Attach and is commit 32's to remove. Claiming this commit makes the VM profile able to host a DOM would be exactly the overreach the plan warns against. 111 UNDER A WIDER METRIC THAN THE 108 IT REPLACES, AND THE TREE GOT BETTER, NOT WORSE. The count now also sees engine namespaces spelled without their Broiler. root -- 23 of them here -- while the same commit deleted 20 dead using lines from the four LayoutMetrics partials and added 2 that JsInterop needs to answer the kind a provider would. Real coupling fell by 18. The DOM bridge. Started at 891 when JSEAL landed, and the name-validation cluster moved -- ThrowDOMException and the three validators now take an IJsRealm and reach IJsCalls.DomError, which the Broiler.JS provider implements with the same algorithm and the same fallback wording, so no page sees a different exception. That commit also removed IAttributesHost.JsContext, whose own doc comment had named the condition for its removal. What remains is structural rather than unmigrated: the three wrapper-root fields DomBridge declares and ten files read; IDomBridgeRuntime.Attach, which takes a JSContext from another project; BridgeModuleContext, which derives from the engine's module context because JSEAL has no module-graph contract; and the event-host surfaces that still type a listener as the engine's function. The weak tables that were recorded here as needing a reference-typed key a struct handle cannot be were a MISTAKE: the struct was never the key, the reference it carries is, and JsValue.ObjectIdentity carried five of them across with no provider change. The ArrayBuffer mint left when IJsValues grew NewArrayBuffer and TryGetArrayBufferBytes, and the Storage delete left when IJsExoticDelete landed -- both were contract gaps rather than unmigrated code, and both closed by adding to JSEAL rather than by working around it here. Each occurrence names its own pin in its doc comment. 60 -> 49 BY DELETION RATHER THAN PORTING, and the shape of what went is the point: four members with no caller anywhere in the tree, two of which carried a doc comment naming the caller they did not have -- IEventTargetHost.DispatchEventOnElement(DomNode, JSObject), the in-Arguments overload of StartSubDocumentViewTransition with its OptionsHandle, and TraversalBinding.GetSelection. Plus three dead locals that no metric could see at all, because a JsInterop crossing names no engine type. THE CLAUSE ABOUT JsObjectRegistry BEING THE WRAPPER-IDENTITY CHOKE POINT IS DELETED HERE: that file was re-typed onto JsValue and measures zero, and three separate investigations quoted this note as their scope statement and inherited the error. 64 -> 60 and 6 -> 5 by deleting rather than porting: DomFunction, superseded when the Broiler.JS provider took createPrototype:false for every member the bridge installs, so its 3 references were paying for a type nothing constructed; a stale using in ElementContentBinding that named the engine and used nothing from it; and RegisterNamedElementGlobals, public, JSContext-typed, carrying one of the eval sites, and with no caller at any point in this repository's history. NOTE FOR ANYONE WRITING PROSE ABOUT THIS METRIC: guestEvalSites is textual and a mention in a comment counts as a call, so the first attempt at DomBridge.cs's replacement comment held the count at 6 by naming the method it was describing. That is the metric working as specified, not a bug in it. 45 -> 44 BY DELETING ONE using LINE, AND THE DEPENDENCY IT NAMED WAS NEVER LOAD-BEARING. DispatchWindowEvent in DomBridge.WindowLoad.cs answered the engine boolean over the engine object, and its doc comment named IWindowEventTargetHost, ILocationHost, DomBridge.MessagingHost.cs and DomBridge/LayoutMetrics.Scrolling.cs as the files that pinned those two types. All four were wrong: the three contracts have declared DispatchWindowEvent(JsValue) since they were extracted, the fourth calls the string overload and throws the answer away, and of the seven call sites the two overloads have between them exactly one reads the return value -- and it converted it to a handle on the same line. The engine object was minted by three bridge-side adapters for no reader but the parameter they were said to pin. One pin was real and it is a call site: InvokeEventListener takes the engine object because EventListenerRegistration is engine-typed in DomBridge/RuntimeStates.cs, so that crossing moved out of three callers into one conversion at the top of the method, taken before the guard so a handle carrying no engine object still fails exactly where it failed before. JsInterop. crossings fall by one on net: three go and one arrives. 48 -> 45, AND THE THIRD ONE WAS NOT PREDICTED. Three files reach 0 here -- DomBridge/LayoutMetrics.Scrolling.cs, Features/TableBinding.cs and Features/FormAssociationBinding.cs -- because in each of them the single counted occurrence was the using line that five deleted members needed. The plan for this commit expected -2, on the ground that LayoutMetrics.Scrolling.cs stays pinned by DispatchVisualViewportScrollEvent. It does not: that method reads the wrapper root through var, and var infers without a using. A SEMANTIC PIN AND A COUNTED REFERENCE ARE NOT THE SAME THING, and this file only ever had the second. NOTHING DELETED HERE WAS DEAD, which is the other half of the shape. Each of the five members had exactly one caller, and each caller reached it by converting a JSEAL handle it already held into the engine object so the callee could convert it straight back: DomBridge/DomBridge.ElementGeometryHost.cs:67,103 for the three scroll-option adapters and DomBridge/ElementInterfaces.cs:103,107,128 for the two installers. Four conversions and five adapters, deleted together, no behaviour anywhere between them. AND THREE COMMENTS DIED WITH THEM, EACH NAMING A CALLER IT DID NOT HAVE. The scroll readers were "shared by every scrolling entry point the bridge has" when their only caller was the element-geometry contract -- the window and sub-window contracts read their own options through a second, static copy in DomBridge.SubWindowHost.cs. The same comment argued the readers cannot be static because "a static has no way to obtain" the realm, which that static pair does by taking it as a parameter. And DomBridge/ElementInterfaces.cs opened on "the two engine namespaces left" while having none, and having had none since ComputedStyleBinding migrated.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal.note: Proved by the compiler, not by this file. The project has no ProjectReference and no PackageReference, so it cannot name an engine type whatever a grep says; the check fails if that project file ever gains one. See the comment in Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal.csproj.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal.BroilerJs.note: The Broiler.JS provider, and the one project under src/ whose budget is not expected to reach zero. Naming Broiler.JavaScript is what this assembly is for: every reference here is a reference the bridge no longer has to make. The single eval site is JSContext.Eval inside the realm's own IJsSource implementation -- the provider being asked to evaluate, not a binding evaluating. Its two engine project references are Broiler.JavaScript.Engine and .BuiltIns. Its engineProjectRefs rose from 2 to 3 when IJsClone landed: JSGlobalStatic.StructuredClone lives in Broiler.JavaScript.Globals, so the provider that implements structured clone needs it. That is the gate doing its job rather than a regression -- the same reference LEFT Broiler.HtmlBridge.Dom in the same commit, because the bridge's only use of it was the call that is now behind the contract. An engine assembly reached by the provider and not by the bridge is the shape all of these should end in.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal.Vm.note: The Broiler.VM provider. It is marked a provider for the same reason the Broiler.JS one is - naming an engine is what a provider is FOR - but its reference count reads 0 rather than a large number, and the zero is a fact about the METRIC and not about this assembly. engineReferences counts occurrences of the string Broiler.JavaScript, which is the Broiler.JS engine namespace; this provider names Broiler.VM.Profile.JavaScript instead, so the count does not see it. The five project references do see it, and they are the honest measure here: Abstractions, Binary, Runtime, the profile, and the profile compiler. Read the 0 as "this assembly names no Broiler.JS type", which is true and worth keeping true, and read the 5 as its engine coupling.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Scripting.note: Five files now: the Broiler.JS ScriptEngine and what it needs to build a realm. InteractiveSession left the count when its constructor stopped taking a JSContext -- it read the context once, to dispose it, so the parameter is typed IDisposable and the class names no engine type at all. That reference was load-bearing for a reason unrelated to what it did: VmScriptEngine named the constructor as half of why the document-bearing overloads are forwarded. This is where the Broiler.JS provider will live once it is one, and the counts here move to a Jseal.BroilerJs assembly rather than to zero -- a provider naming its own engine is what a provider is for.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Scripting.Vm.note: The 1 is a doc comment in VmScriptEngine.cs saying the profile does not expose Broiler.JavaScript types. It is counted because the metric is textual and stays textual: a check that tried to tell prose from code would need a parser, and would then be arguable in a way this is not. Lower it by rewording the sentence, or leave it -- it costs nothing at 1.
